Keywords: Maker, From, Thy

outputs.L1:
**Maker of Sevens**

Maker of sevens in the scheme of things,  
From earth to star,  
Thy cycle holds whatever is fate—  
And, over the border, the bar.  

Though rank and fierce, the mariner,  
Sailing the seven seas,  
Prays as he holds his glass to his eyes,  
Coaxing the Pleiades.  

I cannot love them; and I feel your glad  
Chiding from the grave:  
That my all was only worth, after all,  
The joy to you it gave.  

These seven links the Law compelled  
For the human chain—  
I cannot love them; and you, oh,  
Sevenfold months in Flanders slain!  

A jungle there, a cave here, bred—  
Through six and a million years—  
Sure and strong, mate for mate, such love  
As culture fears.  

I gave you clear the oil and wine;  
You saved me your hob and hearth—  
See how even life may be, ere the Sickle  
Comes and leaves a swath.  

But I can wait the seven of moons,  
Or years I spare,  
Hoarding the heart’s plenty, nor spend  
A drop, nor share—  

So long as there outlives a smile  
And a silken gown;  
Then gaily I reach up from my shroud,  
And you, glory-clad, reach down.
outputs.L2:
Shaper of sevens in the cosmic plan,  
Stretching from soil to stars,  
Your turning circle encloses all destiny  
And sets the boundary’s gate.

However proud and fearless the sailor  
Who crosses all seven oceans,  
He raises his telescope and pleads,  
Trying to draw the Pleiades near.

I cannot cherish them, and from the grave  
I sense your cheerful reproach:  
Everything I possessed had value only  
Through the happiness it brought you.

The Law ordained these seven joining rings  
For humanity’s chain—  
Yet I cannot love them, nor you,  
Seven months dead in Flanders!

One was formed in jungle, another in cave,  
Across six million years,  
Each steadfast and powerful, perfectly matched—  
A love that civilization dreads.

I freely offered you oil and wine;  
You kept your fireside and home for me.  
See how balanced life can become before  
The Sickle falls and cuts its path.

Still, I can endure seven moons—  
Or even seven years—  
Storing the heart’s abundance without using  
Or sharing a single drop,

Provided only that a smile and  
A silk dress survive me.  
Then, joyful, I will rise from my burial cloth,  
While you, clothed in glory, bend down.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents the number seven as a recurring and symbolic force governing fate, nature, time, and human life. This pattern gives the speaker’s grief a sense of inevitability, as though both love and loss belong to a larger cosmic order. At the heart of the poem is the speaker’s mourning for a beloved person who was killed after seven months in Flanders. Faced with this devastating loss, the speaker struggles to accept—and even more painfully, to love—the bonds and limitations imposed by fate.

The relationship between the speaker and the beloved is portrayed as powerful, instinctive, and deeply rooted. Their love endured despite the fears, expectations, and restrictions associated with civilized society. It offered both people a source of strength and freedom, allowing them to remain emotionally connected even in a world shaped by anxiety, conflict, and external pressures.

The speaker also remembers the relationship as a balanced exchange of affection and support. Each person gave the other gifts, comfort, and joy, creating a sense of mutual completeness. These shared experiences made life feel harmonious and meaningful before death abruptly disturbed that balance.

Although the beloved is gone, memory continues to sustain the speaker. Grief is tempered by hope, particularly the belief that death is not the final end of their bond. The poem therefore moves toward an expectation of reunion: the speaker waits for the moment beyond the grave when separation will end and the joy they once shared will be restored.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents love as a force that exists within—and perhaps beyond—the vast patterns of fate, time, and mortality. Its recurring use of the number seven gives the work a symbolic structure, suggesting completion, destiny, and the cyclical nature of existence. This pattern is reinforced by images of cosmic movement, historical change, and evolution, all of which place the lovers’ experience within a much larger story. Their relationship is not isolated from the world; instead, it unfolds amid the immense processes that shape life, from the birth and death of stars to the rise and fall of civilizations.

Against this vast background, human love may appear fragile and temporary. War, separation, loss, and death repeatedly threaten to destroy the bond between the lovers. The poem acknowledges that suffering is unavoidable and that time changes both individuals and societies. Yet these destructive forces do not entirely erase what love has created. Memory preserves moments of happiness, while the recurring cycles of the poem suggest that endings may also contain the possibility of renewal. Separation therefore becomes not only a source of grief but also a test of love’s endurance.

The poem ultimately argues that love does not need to be permanent in an ordinary, physical sense in order to possess lasting value. Its worth lies partly in the joy it gives while it is experienced. Even if the lovers are divided by circumstance, violence, or death, that joy remains meaningful because it has transformed their lives. Love becomes a form of resistance to despair: it cannot prevent mortality, but it can give purpose and beauty to a mortal existence.

By connecting personal affection with cosmic cycles and repeated patterns of destruction and rebirth, the poem leaves open the hope of reunion. Such a reunion may occur through memory, through the renewal of life, or in a spiritual realm beyond time and death. The conclusion is therefore both sorrowful and hopeful. Loss is real, but it is not necessarily final. Love survives through the happiness it has given, the identity it has shaped, and the faith it inspires in a transcendent future where separation may finally be overcome.
outputs.L5:
**From Thy Hands, Maker**

Maker of dawn and distant stars,  
from Thy hands all wonders rise.  
You shape the mountains, stir the seas,  
and breathe new hope into weary hearts.

From silence, Thou bringest music;  
from darkness, light.  
Teach us, Maker, to cherish Thy creation  
and to shape our lives with kindness, courage, and love.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an elegiac poem in an archaic, Kipling-like style about love, fate, the number seven, and a beloved killed in Flanders.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Seventh Star**

O seven were the roads we knew,  
And seven the bells of morn;  
Seven the vows I swore to you  
Beside the ripening corn.  
But Fate, that weigheth king and clown  
Nor heedeth prayer nor plea,  
Set one black road to Flanders town,  
And six led home to me.

Thy letter bore a Flemish stain,  
Thy hand was firm and small:  
*“When seven stars shine out again,  
I shall have passed them all.”*  
Ah, Love may reckon kiss and tear,  
And Hope her beads may tell—  
But Death hath neither month nor year,  
And keepeth silence well.

They found thee where the poppies blowed  
Above the shattered clay,  
Thy face turned homeward on the road  
That never came this way.  
No priestly word, no muffled drum,  
No banner wrapped thy breast;  
Only the guns that bade thee come  
Spake thunder o’er thy rest.

Now seven candles do I light  
When autumn nights are long;  
Six burn pale against the night—  
The seventh burneth strong.  
For six are grief, and dust, and doom,  
And years that will not cease;  
But one is Love beyond the tomb,  
And one is God’s own peace.

So bide thou there in Flanders ground,  
Where iron harvests lie;  
Though Fate hath drawn her circle round,  
Love breaketh it—or I.  
And when the seventh trumpet saith  
That earth shall loose her slain,  
I’ll find thee past the gates of Death,  
And count thee mine again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue spoken by a grieving widow who reflects on seven months of marriage, wartime loss, and reunion after death.
counterfactuals.output:
Seven months.

They call it brief—as though love were measured by the calendar, as though seven months beside you could be weighed against the long, gray years they say remain to me. Seven months a wife, and now a widow. Two words, and a war between them.

Do you remember our wedding morning? It rained before the bells. You said the sky was weeping for joy, and I laughed because your hands were trembling worse than mine. We had so little: two rooms, a cracked blue cup, a table that leaned toward the window. Yet every night, when you crossed the threshold, the whole house stood straight.

Then came the summons.

You folded it once. Only once. I watched your thumb smooth the crease, as if gentleness might alter what was written there. We spoke bravely after that. Such fine speeches we made! Duty. Honor. A swift return. We dressed our terror in splendid words and pretended not to know it.

At the station, you kissed me before them all.

“Seven months,” I whispered.

“A beginning,” you said.

And then the train carried you away.

Your letters came stained with rain and mud. You wrote of everything except fear: the bad coffee, the lice, the moon above the trenches. You asked if the roses had opened. You asked whether the roof still leaked. You asked me to keep your place beside the fire.

I kept it.

Even when the telegram came, I kept it.

The officer said you died at dawn. He said you were brave. He said you did not suffer. Men always bring those phrases to widows, polished smooth by use, as though bravery could warm an empty bed, as though a painless death were not still death.

I thanked him. Can you imagine? I thanked him for telling me the world had ended.

They gave me no grave to kneel beside. Only your name cut into stone among thousands, each letter neat and cold. I laid my hand upon it and tried to feel your pulse.

Nothing.

Yet sometimes, just before sleep, I hear your key turn in the door. I smell rain on your coat. The mattress bends beneath your weight, and for one merciful breath I am not alone. Then morning comes, cruel and punctual, and I am a widow again.

But listen, my love: death has only made me wait.

Let the years come. Let them silver my hair and bend my back. Let this war pass into history, its guns rusted, its banners dust. I will carry our seven months through every season they deny us. I will guard them like seven bright candles in a ruined church.

And when my own last dawn arrives, do not send angels to meet me. Do not send choirs or trumpets.

Come yourself.

Stand as you stood beneath the station clock, young and frightened and trying to smile. Reach out your hand. I shall know it, though heaven has remade us both.

Then we will go home—not to the two small rooms, nor the cracked blue cup, nor the chair beside the fire, but to the life that waited beyond the seventh month. No telegram will find us there. No train will carry you from me.

And I will say, “You took so long.”

And you will answer, as you did before:

“My darling, this is only the beginning.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a rhyming Victorian-style elegy in which “seven” recurs as a motif and the speaker addresses a dead lover from beyond the grave?
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Seventh Bell**

Belovèd, when the seventh bell  
Grows faint along the rain,  
I call thee from the graveyard dell,  
Though earth entombs my pain.  

Seven pale stars above thee keep  
Their vigil, cold and white;  
Yet none may pierce thy dreamless sleep,  
Nor warm thy shrouded night.  

Seven long years I wore thy ring,  
Seven roses graced thy door;  
Now seven winds of winter sing  
Where we shall meet no more.  

I speak beneath the churchyard stone,  
Where root and shadow twine;  
Though thou art dead, thou art not lone—  
Thy silent dust seeks mine.  

Dost thou recall the seventh day,  
Beneath the mournful yew,  
When Death in sable bore thee away,  
And broke my spirit too?  

Then hear me, love: at midnight’s fall,  
When seven echoes start,  
My ghost shall pass the iron wall  
And kneel beside thy heart.  

Till seven seas forsake the shore,  
Till Heaven’s last lamp is riven,  
I shall adore thee evermore—  
My lost, my only heaven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, old-fashioned poem about cosmic cycles, sailors, marriage, grief, patience, and two lovers reaching toward each other from life and death.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Epithalamium of the Turning Spheres**

When Saturn, with his leaden-lidded star,  
Hath told the widow’d ages bead by bead,  
And hornèd moons, like shallops from afar,  
Freight heaven’s black tide with phosphorescent seed,  
The dead suns kindle; spent creation heaves,  
And Time rebinds the sheaf himself unweaves.

So mariners, beneath the polar flame,  
Through whale-road, wrack, and trumpet-throated gale,  
Commit their bones unto no certain name,  
But court one harbour past the utmost sail;  
Each keeps, sewn inward where the cold seas start,  
A little compass trembling toward a heart.

O Marriage, ancient anchor, golden yoke,  
Two solitudes by solemn promise tied!  
Thy candle gutters, yet outlives the smoke;  
Thy bed is narrow as the grave is wide.  
There hand takes hand, though all the bells of breath  
Ring noon for one, for one the dusk of death.

She, on the greenward margin of the day,  
Grows grey with waiting, patient as the stone;  
He, where the drowned constellations stray,  
Hears through the earth her pulse’s muffled tone.  
Grief is the sea betwixt them—salt and vast—  
Yet love, that oldest sailor, sounds its mast.

“Reach down,” he cries, from death’s becalmèd deep,  
Where asphodels like pallid lanterns burn.  
“Reach up,” saith she, who hath not learn’d to weep  
Without believing tears themselves return.  
Their fingers strain through root, through shroud, through sphere—  
Not touching; yet no touch was e’er so near.

For patience is no meek, unbloodied dove,  
But Jacob wrestling till the dark be done;  
A mast bow’d double, yet upheld above  
The furious plural waters, one by one.  
It keeps the ring, though flesh and flower depart,  
And wears eternity against the heart.

At last the wheeling firmament shall close;  
The serpent Year shall taste his tail again;  
The same old spring awake the selfsame rose,  
The same two vessels breast the selfsame main.  
Then life shall lean from dawn, death climb from night,  
And their long-sever’d hands make one world bright.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
